items.q: What is a PMS?
items.a: A Portfolio Management Service is a SEBI-registered manager running a portfolio of stocks (and sometimes bonds or funds) for you, held in a demat account in your own name. Unlike a mutual fund, you own the shares directly and the portfolio can be concentrated, often 15 to 30 stocks. The minimum is ₹50 lakh.

items.q: What is the minimum investment for a PMS?
items.a: SEBI sets the minimum at ₹50 lakh per client, in cash or existing shares. If you have less, look at mutual funds, the new ₹10 lakh Specialised Investment Funds, or the ₹25 lakh PRIM route for managed mutual fund portfolios.

items.q: How is a PMS different from a mutual fund?
items.a: In a PMS you own the shares directly, the portfolio is more concentrated, fees are higher and can include a share of profits, and the minimum is ₹50 lakh. A mutual fund pools money from many investors, is more diversified, costs less, and starts from ₹100 or ₹500. Tax also works differently: in a PMS every trade the manager makes can create a taxable gain for you.

items.q: What is the difference between discretionary and non-discretionary PMS?
items.a: In a discretionary PMS the manager buys and sells without asking you each time. In a non-discretionary PMS the manager recommends and you approve each trade. In an advisory PMS the manager only advises and you execute. Most PMS money in India is discretionary.

items.q: Who regulates PMS in India?
items.a: SEBI regulates portfolio managers under its Portfolio Managers Regulations. In September 2026 SEBI's board approved new 2026 regulations replacing the 2020 rules. The industry body is APMI, which also publishes standardised performance data that NIVO uses.

items.q: Do I own the shares in a PMS?
items.a: Yes. The shares sit in a demat account opened in your name. The manager operates it under your agreement, but your holdings are not pooled with other clients'. That's why you can see every stock you own.

items.q: Is a PMS safer than a mutual fund?
items.a: No. A PMS is usually riskier, because it holds fewer stocks and can take bigger bets. Its regulation is strong, but a concentrated portfolio can fall harder than a diversified fund. Choose a PMS for conviction and personalisation, not for safety.

items.q: Can I invest in a PMS with existing shares?
items.a: Yes. Most managers accept shares you already hold as part of the ₹50 lakh, valued at market price. The manager may sell the ones that don't fit their strategy, which can create a capital-gains tax bill for you. Ask before you transfer.

items.q: How long should I stay invested in a PMS?
items.a: Plan for at least 3 to 5 years. Strategies go through long spells of trailing their index, and judging a manager on one or two years usually leads to switching at the wrong time. Money you need within 3 years should not be in a PMS.

items.q: Can a PMS manager invest in IPOs or foreign shares?
items.a: Under the 2026 rules approved by SEBI's board, portfolio managers can invest in IPOs, primary debt issues and some foreign securities, subject to conditions. Ask your manager whether their strategy uses these, and how much.

items.q: What is a model portfolio in a PMS?
items.a: Most PMS strategies run one model portfolio that every client's account copies. Your account can differ from the model because of when you joined, cash flows and timing. That's why your actual return can differ from the strategy's reported return.

items.q: Why is my PMS return different from the reported return?
items.a: Reported strategy returns are for the model portfolio. Your account differs if you joined at a different time, added or withdrew money, transferred in shares, or paid a performance fee at a different point. Ask the manager for your own client-level return, after all fees.

items.q: What is a PMS disclosure document?
items.a: A document every portfolio manager must give you before you sign. It covers the strategy, the risks, all fees and charges, the manager's background, and past performance. Read the fees section closely: it is where costs hide.

items.q: What happens to my PMS if the portfolio manager shuts down?
items.a: Your shares are in a demat account in your name, so they don't vanish with the manager. You would move to another manager or take the shares into your own demat. SEBI has proposed making PMS demat accounts portable to make switching easier.

items.q: Can NRIs invest in a PMS?
items.a: Yes, many managers accept NRIs, usually through NRE or NRO accounts with extra paperwork and repatriation rules. Not every manager onboards NRIs digitally. Ask the manager about NRI onboarding and tax withholding before you start.

items.q: How do I choose a good PMS?
items.a: Start with your IPS: how much risk you can take and how long you can wait. Then compare strategies on returns after fees against their closest index, how they handled falls, consistency, and how long they have been running. NIVO's “Find my right PMS” does this for you and suggests your top 5.

items.q: Which is the best PMS in India?
items.a: There is no single best PMS. The right one depends on your risk, horizon and what else you own. NIVO ranks every strategy on its NIVO Score, and “Find my right PMS” matches the top 5 to your own answers. Past returns alone are a poor guide.

items.q: Is a high return over 1 year a good reason to pick a PMS?
items.a: No. One year is mostly luck and market style. Look at 3 and 5 year returns against the closest index, how it did in falls, and whether it beat its index consistently. The strategy with last year's top return is often not the leader next year.

items.q: What questions should I ask a PMS manager before investing?
items.a: Ask: what are the fees in rupees on my amount, including performance fee, hurdle and exit load? What was the biggest fall from peak and how long did recovery take? What is the median client's actual return? How many stocks, and how much in small caps? How much of it overlaps with my mutual funds?

items.q: How many PMS should I hold?
items.a: Most investors need one or two, in different styles, for example one large or flexi cap and one mid and small cap. More than three usually adds overlap and fees without adding diversification. Keep the rest of your money in mutual funds, debt and cash as your IPS says.

items.q: What is a good NIVO Score for a PMS?
items.a: NIVO Score runs from 0 to 10 and compares each strategy with its peers. Above 7 is strong, 5 to 7 is middling, below 5 is weak. Strategies with under 3 years of record are pulled toward the middle, because short records say little.

items.q: Should I pick a PMS with a short track record?
items.a: Be careful. With under 3 years, you can't tell skill from a good market. If you like a new manager, keep it to a small part of your PMS money and judge it over a full cycle. NIVO flags strategies with under 3 years of record.

items.q: What is style drift in a PMS?
items.a: Style drift is when a strategy sold as one style, say large cap, starts behaving like another, say mid and small cap. It can raise your risk without you noticing. NIVO's Style check compares each strategy's yearly returns with indices to flag possible drift.

items.q: Large cap PMS or mid and small cap PMS?
items.a: Large cap PMS usually falls less and recovers faster, but has a harder time beating cheap index funds. Mid and small cap PMS can grow faster but can fall 30% or more and stay down for years. Pick by your horizon and your real reaction to falls, not by last year's returns.

items.q: Is a PMS worth it compared with a good mutual fund?
items.a: Only if the strategy beats a comparable low-cost fund after all fees, over full cycles, and you value owning the stocks directly. Many PMS strategies don't. NIVO's mutual fund twin shows what a same-style fund portfolio did, so you can judge the gap.

items.q: What is a multi-asset PMS?
items.a: A strategy that mixes equity with debt, gold or funds, aiming for smoother returns. It suits investors who want professional management but can't sit through deep equity falls. Returns are usually lower than pure equity strategies over long periods.

items.q: How do I compare a PMS with its benchmark?
items.a: Compare returns after fees with the index closest to its style: Nifty 50 for large cap, Nifty 500 for flexi cap, midcap and smallcap indices for mid and small cap. NIVO picks the closest index for every strategy and shows both side by side.

items.q: What does consistency mean in PMS ratings?
items.a: How often the strategy beat its index or peers across many periods, not just overall. A strategy that beat the index in 80% of periods is more dependable than one that beat it hugely once and lagged otherwise.

items.q: What is a volatility index in NIVO?
items.a: NIVO's volatility index runs from 0 to 10 and compares a fund or PMS with its closest index over 5 years. 5 means it moves like the index. Higher is calmer than the index; lower is bumpier. It uses swings, the biggest fall and how much of the index's falls it caught.

items.q: Should I follow a famous fund manager to their PMS?
items.a: A famous name is not a strategy. Check the actual strategy's record, fees, concentration and whether the star manager runs it day to day. Also check key-person risk: what happens if they leave.

items.q: What fees does a PMS charge?
items.a: Usually a fixed management fee each year, a performance fee (a share of gains above a hurdle), and sometimes an exit load in the first years. There are also brokerage, custody and fund accounting charges. Ask for all of them in rupees on your amount.

items.q: What is a hurdle rate in a PMS?
items.a: The return the strategy must beat before the manager earns a performance fee, for example 10% a year. Check whether it is calculated on a high-water mark, so you don't pay twice for recovering the same loss.

items.q: What is a high-water mark?
items.a: The highest value your account has reached. With a high-water mark, the manager earns a performance fee only on gains above that peak. Without it, you could pay a fee for simply recovering an earlier loss.

items.q: Can a PMS charge an exit load?
items.a: Yes, but only in the first three years, and SEBI caps how much. After the third year, no exit load is allowed. Ask for the exact exit load schedule before you sign.

items.q: Are PMS returns shown before or after fees?
items.a: Since SEBI's 2020 rules, PMS performance is reported after all fees and expenses. Your own account can still differ from the reported figure because of timing and when fees are charged.

items.q: How much does a mutual fund cost?
items.a: Through its expense ratio, taken daily from the fund's value. Direct plans have lower expense ratios than Regular plans, because Regular plans include the distributor's commission. You never see a bill: it shows up as a slightly lower return.

items.q: What is the difference between Direct and Regular plans?
items.a: Same fund, same manager, same stocks. The Regular plan pays a distributor commission every year out of your returns; the Direct plan doesn't. Over 10 to 20 years the gap compounds into lakhs. NIVO's Commission X-ray shows what you're paying.

items.q: How much do commissions cost me over 20 years?
items.a: Roughly, a 1% yearly cost on ₹10 lakh growing at 11% takes away close to ₹15 to 17 lakh of growth over 20 years. Import your CAS statement and NIVO's Commission X-ray calculates your own number.

items.q: Why do advisers recommend Regular plans?
items.a: Because Regular plans pay the distributor a trail commission every year. That isn't always bad: you may get service in return. But you should know what it costs. A SEBI-registered investment adviser can't take commissions and must recommend Direct plans.

items.q: Is a 1% advisory fee on AUM reasonable?
items.a: It depends on what you get. On ₹1 crore, 1% is ₹1 lakh a year, every year, growing as your money grows. For individuals and HUFs, SEBI caps a registered adviser's fee at ₹1.51 lakh a year per family in fixed-fee mode, or 2.5% of assets advised. Compare the fee with the advice you actually receive.

items.q: What hidden costs should I look for in a PMS?
items.a: Brokerage on every trade, custody and depository charges, fund accounting fees, GST on all fees, and the performance fee. High portfolio turnover also creates short-term capital gains tax. Ask for last year's total costs as a percentage of the average portfolio.

items.q: Does NIVO take commission?
items.a: No. NIVO takes no commission, no referral fee and no paid placement, and its rankings can't be bought. When execution goes live, it will place orders only in Direct plans and use direct onboarding for PMS.

items.q: What does a distributor earn from a PMS?
items.a: Since 2020, PMS distributors can only receive trail commission paid out of the manager's fees, not upfront commission. Distributors must be registered with APMI. You can avoid the distributor completely through direct onboarding.

items.q: What is direct onboarding in a PMS?
items.a: SEBI requires every portfolio manager to let you invest directly, without a distributor. You deal with the manager, and there are no charges other than statutory ones for onboarding. Ask for “direct onboarding” and the digital sign-up link.

items.q: How do I check what I'm paying in my mutual funds?
items.a: Download your CAS (consolidated account statement) from CAMS, KFintech, NSDL or CDSL and import it into NIVO. The Commission X-ray lists every Regular plan, what it costs you each year, and its Direct twin.

items.q: What is a mutual fund?
items.a: A fund that pools money from many investors and invests it in shares, bonds or both, run by a SEBI-registered fund house. You own units whose value (NAV) moves with the investments. You can start with small amounts and sell on any working day.

items.q: What is NAV?
items.a: Net Asset Value: the value of one unit of a fund, calculated each working day after costs. A low NAV doesn't mean a fund is cheap; it only reflects when the fund started and how it has grown.

items.q: What is a flexi cap fund?
items.a: An equity fund that can invest across large, mid and small companies in any proportion. It gives the manager freedom to shift with opportunities. Good as a core holding for long-term investors.

items.q: What is the difference between flexi cap and multi cap funds?
items.a: A multi cap fund must keep at least 25% each in large, mid and small caps. A flexi cap fund can move freely. Multi cap funds tend to carry more small-cap risk at all times.

items.q: What is a large and mid cap fund?
items.a: A fund that must hold at least 35% in large caps and 35% in mid caps. It sits between a pure large cap fund and a mid cap fund in risk.

items.q: Are index funds better than active funds?
items.a: In large caps, low-cost index funds have been hard to beat after costs. In mid and small caps, good active managers have more room to add value. Many investors use an index fund as the core and active funds around it.

items.q: What is a debt fund?
items.a: A fund that invests in bonds, government securities and money-market instruments. It is not a fixed deposit: its value can fall when interest rates rise or a borrower defaults. Choose by how long you'll hold it and the credit quality.

items.q: Which debt fund for money needed in 1 year?
items.a: Short-term money suits liquid, money market or ultra short duration funds, which carry little interest-rate risk. For tax reasons, some investors in high brackets prefer arbitrage funds. Check exit loads and current tax rules.

items.q: What is a target maturity fund?
items.a: A debt fund that holds bonds maturing around a fixed date and winds up then. If you hold to maturity, returns are fairly predictable. Selling early can mean losses if rates have risen.

items.q: What is an arbitrage fund?
items.a: A fund that earns the small price gap between the cash and futures markets. Returns are similar to liquid funds with low risk, and it is taxed like an equity fund. Useful for parking money for a few months.

items.q: What is a balanced advantage fund?
items.a: A hybrid fund that moves between equity and debt based on market valuations. It aims for smoother returns than pure equity. Results vary a lot between fund houses, so compare their models.

items.q: What is a SIP?
items.a: A Systematic Investment Plan: investing a fixed amount every month into a fund. It builds discipline and buys more units when prices are low. A SIP doesn't remove risk: it spreads your entry points.

items.q: Is SIP better than lump sum?
items.a: If you already have the money, history shows lump sum has usually done better over long periods, because money is invested sooner. A SIP or a staggered plan over 6 to 12 months reduces regret if markets fall right after you invest. Choose the one you'll stick with.

items.q: Should I stop my SIP when markets fall?
items.a: Usually no. Falls are when your SIP buys the most units for the same money. Stopping locks in the bad months and skips the cheap ones. Only stop if you need the cash or your goal has changed.

items.q: How many mutual funds should I own?
items.a: Usually 4 to 7 is plenty: an index or large cap core, one or two flexi or mid cap funds, maybe one small cap, and debt and liquid funds as needed. More funds usually means overlap, not diversification.

items.q: What is portfolio overlap?
items.a: When several of your funds hold the same stocks. Five funds that all own the same top 20 stocks give you little diversification. Check overlap before adding a fund.

items.q: What is an ELSS fund?
items.a: An equity fund with a 3-year lock-in that has qualified for tax deductions under the old tax regime. Whether it still saves tax depends on the regime you choose. Treat it as an equity fund first.

items.q: What is a Specialised Investment Fund (SIF)?
items.a: A new product from 2025, run by mutual fund houses under mutual fund rules, allowing strategies such as long-short. The minimum is ₹10 lakh per PAN across a fund house's SIF strategies. It sits between mutual funds and PMS.

items.q: What is PRIM?
items.a: The Portfolio Managers' Route for Investing in Mutual Fund units, approved by SEBI's board in September 2026. A portfolio manager builds and manages a portfolio of Direct mutual funds for you, from ₹25 lakh, with the fixed fee capped at 1% a year.

items.q: What is an AIF?
items.a: An Alternative Investment Fund: a privately pooled fund for things like private equity, venture capital, private credit or long-short strategies. The minimum is generally ₹1 crore, money is often locked in, and it suits experienced, wealthy investors.

items.q: What is an IPS?
items.a: An Investment Policy Statement: a short written plan of your goals, horizon, risk limits, asset allocation and rules for when to change things. It keeps you from making decisions on emotion. NIVO builds one in six steps.

items.q: Why do I need an IPS?
items.a: Because most investing mistakes happen in the moment: buying after a rally, selling in a crash, chasing a friend's tip. An IPS writes your rules down when you're calm, so you can check every decision against them.

items.q: What is asset allocation?
items.a: How you split money between equity, debt, gold and cash. It explains most of how your portfolio behaves, more than which individual funds you pick. Set it first, then choose products to fill each slot.

items.q: How much equity should I have?
items.a: It depends on your horizon, your capacity to take risk and how you behave in falls. A rough starting point is 15% plus three-quarters of your risk score, capped lower for short horizons. NIVO's IPS works this out for you and stress-tests it against a 2020-style crash.

items.q: What is risk capacity versus risk tolerance?
items.a: Capacity is how much loss your finances can absorb: income, savings, dependants, horizon. Tolerance is how much loss you can stomach emotionally. NIVO uses the lower of the two plus a little of the gap, because either one can force a bad sale.

items.q: How often should I rebalance?
items.a: Check once a year, and rebalance when any slot drifts more than about 5 percentage points from target. Use new money first to avoid selling and paying tax. After a 20% market fall, review the whole plan.

items.q: How much emergency fund do I need?
items.a: Commonly 6 months of expenses, more if your income is irregular or you support others. Keep it in a savings account, FD or liquid fund. Build it before investing in a PMS.

items.q: Should I pay off my loan or invest?
items.a: Compare the loan's interest rate with what you can reasonably expect after tax. High-rate loans like credit cards and personal loans almost always come first. A low-rate home loan can sit alongside long-term investing.

items.q: How much do I need to retire?
items.a: A common starting point is 25 to 30 times your yearly expenses at retirement, adjusted for inflation between now and then. The exact number depends on pension, health costs and how long you'll need the money. Set it as a goal in your IPS and NIVO shows whether you're on track.

items.q: How do I invest for my child's education?
items.a: Work out today's cost, grow it at education inflation to the year you need it, and invest accordingly: more equity when it's 10+ years away, shifting to debt in the last 3 years. Don't use a PMS for money needed on a fixed date soon.

items.q: What return should I expect from equity?
items.a: Nobody can promise one. Long-run Indian equity returns have been around low double digits, with years of losses in between. NIVO uses 11% for core equity only as a planning assumption, never a promise.

items.q: How should a first-time investor start?
items.a: Build an emergency fund, get health and term cover, then start a SIP in a low-cost index or flexi cap fund. Write a simple IPS. Add complexity like PMS only when you have ₹50 lakh to invest and have lived through a market fall.

items.q: I'm moving from mutual funds to PMS. What should I check?
items.a: Check that the PMS adds something your funds don't, that you're comfortable with 15 to 30 stocks, that you understand the fee structure in rupees, and that your PMS money is no more than about half your investments. Run “Find my right PMS” first.

items.q: What should an HNI do differently?
items.a: Think in terms of the whole family balance sheet: concentration in your business or property, liquidity for taxes and opportunities, succession, and costs at scale. A 1% fee on a large portfolio is a big rupee number, so make every layer of cost earn its place.

items.q: What is a model portfolio?
items.a: A ready-made mix that shows how to split money across categories for a given risk level. NIVO has Aggressive, Balanced and Conservative models from its research team, filled with the best-scored Direct fund in each category.

items.q: The market fell 10%. Should I sell?
items.a: Check three things before acting: does your plan say you need this money soon, has anything changed about your goals, and has your portfolio drifted beyond its bands? If not, a fall is usually a time to hold or rebalance, not sell. NIVO's Panic guard reminds you of your own rules.

items.q: My PMS is down 25%. What should I do?
items.a: First compare with its index: if the index fell similarly, the manager is doing what the style does. Check whether the manager's process or team changed. If neither, selling now usually locks in the loss. If you can't sleep, your allocation may be too aggressive for you: fix it gradually.

items.q: My PMS has trailed the Nifty for 18 months. Should I switch?
items.a: Not on that alone. Most good strategies go through 1 to 2 year spells of trailing their index. Switch if the process, team or style has changed, or after a full 3 to 5 year cycle of trailing. Switching after a bad spell often means buying last year's winner just before it cools.

items.q: A friend made 60% in a small-cap PMS. Should I move?
items.a: Ask what risk produced that 60%. Small-cap strategies that rise that fast can fall 40% just as fast. Stick to the style that fits your plan; chasing last year's winner is one of the most expensive habits in investing.

items.q: Is now a good time to invest?
items.a: Nobody can time markets reliably. If your horizon is long, invest per your plan; if you're nervous, stagger a lump sum over 6 to 12 months. Waiting for a fall often means missing the rise.

items.q: Should I wait for a correction before investing?
items.a: Corrections come, but nobody knows when or from what level. Investors who wait often buy higher than where they started waiting. Staggering your entry is a better compromise than waiting.

items.q: Why do I feel like selling when markets fall?
items.a: Losses hurt about twice as much as equal gains feel good. That's normal. The fix is to decide your rules while calm, keep money you need soon out of equity, and look at your portfolio less often during falls.

items.q: How do I avoid panic selling?
items.a: Write your rules down in an IPS, keep 3 years of planned spending outside equity, avoid checking prices daily in a fall, and use NIVO's Panic guard before any sale. Most panic sales happen within days of a big headline.

items.q: My family says shares are gambling. What should I tell them?
items.a: Explain the plan, not the market: why this money is long-term, how much is kept safe, and how a diversified portfolio differs from betting on single stocks. Share your IPS. Their worry is about losing money you need, so show them that money is protected.

items.q: Should I book profits after a big rally?
items.a: Only if your allocation has drifted beyond its band, or you need the money. Rebalancing back to target trims winners in a disciplined way. Selling everything after a rally often means sitting in cash while markets keep rising.

items.q: What is a drawdown?
items.a: The fall from a portfolio's peak to its lowest point before it recovers. A 30% drawdown needs a 43% gain to get back. Knowing past drawdowns tells you what to expect in the next bad year.

items.q: How long do markets take to recover from a crash?
items.a: It varies a lot. Some falls recovered within a year, others took several years, and individual funds and stocks may never fully recover. That's why money needed within 3 years should not be in equity.

items.q: Should I check my portfolio every day?
items.a: No. Daily checking makes normal ups and downs feel like losses and pushes you to act. Once a month is plenty; a proper review once a year is enough for most long-term investors.

items.q: What is FOMO in investing?
items.a: Fear of missing out: the urge to buy whatever has just gone up because others are making money. It usually leads to buying high. A written plan and a cooling-off rule of a few days before any new purchase help.

items.q: Is it OK to do nothing in a falling market?
items.a: Often it's the best choice, as long as your plan is sound and your short-term money is safe. Doing nothing isn't neglect: it's following a plan you made when you could think clearly.

items.q: How is a PMS taxed?
items.a: You are taxed as if you bought and sold the shares yourself. Every sale by the manager can create short or long-term capital gains in your name, and dividends are taxed in your hands. High-turnover strategies can create a bigger tax bill. Rules change, so confirm current rates with your CA.

items.q: How are mutual funds taxed?
items.a: Gains are taxed when you sell, and the rate depends on the type of fund and how long you held it. Equity funds and debt funds are taxed differently. Since tax rules change often, check the current rates with your CA before you sell.

items.q: Is switching from a Regular plan to a Direct plan taxable?
items.a: Yes. A switch is treated as selling one plan and buying another, so any gain is taxable and an exit load may apply. Switching units held long enough, or in steps each year, can reduce the tax.

items.q: Does a PMS or mutual fund suit me better for tax?
items.a: Mutual funds don't tax you on the manager's trades inside the fund; you pay only when you sell your units. In a PMS, every trade can be taxable for you. If tax is a big concern, compare after-tax returns, not just reported returns.

items.q: Should taxes stop me from rebalancing?
items.a: Not completely, but they matter. Rebalance with new money first, then with units that carry the least tax, and spread big moves across financial years. A small drift is usually cheaper to tolerate than a big tax bill.

items.q: Can I offset losses against gains?
items.a: Generally capital losses can be set off against capital gains under specific rules, and some can be carried forward. The rules are detailed, so ask your CA before selling for tax purposes.

items.q: Is income from arbitrage funds taxed like equity?
items.a: Arbitrage funds have historically been taxed as equity funds, which made them popular with high-bracket investors for short-term parking. Confirm the current treatment before relying on it.

items.q: Do I pay tax on SIPs every month?
items.a: No. Tax is due only when you sell units. Each SIP instalment counts as a separate purchase, so when you sell, each instalment's holding period is counted from its own date.

items.q: Is NIVO a SEBI-registered investment adviser?
items.a: Not yet. NIVO is a research and analysis tool today. Personalised advice and live execution will start only once NIVO is registered with SEBI as an investment adviser. Until then, use NIVO to question advice, not replace it where you need professional guidance.

items.q: What is a SEBI-registered investment adviser (RIA)?
items.a: A person or firm registered with SEBI to give investment advice for a fee. RIAs can't take commissions from products, must have a written agreement with you, and can help execute only in Direct plans without charging for it.

items.q: How much can an investment adviser charge me?
items.a: For individuals and HUFs, SEBI caps fees at ₹1.51 lakh a year per family in fixed-fee mode, or 2.5% of assets under advice. Different terms can apply for accredited investors and non-individual clients.

items.q: Can my adviser also sell me products?
items.a: Not to the same client. SEBI requires client-level segregation: a firm can either advise you for a fee or distribute products to you for commission, not both.

items.q: What is APMI?
items.a: The Association of Portfolio Managers in India, the PMS industry body. It publishes standardised performance data for strategies, and since January 2025 every PMS distributor must be registered with it.

items.q: How do I check if a PMS or adviser is registered?
items.a: Search SEBI's website for registered intermediaries by name or registration number. Every genuine portfolio manager and adviser has a SEBI registration number they should share readily.

items.q: Someone is promising guaranteed 3% a month. Is it safe?
items.a: No genuine market investment can guarantee returns like that. Promises of fixed high returns, pressure to act fast, or requests to transfer money to a personal account are classic signs of a scam. Check SEBI registration and walk away.

items.q: Should I give my demat login or OTP to a manager?
items.a: Never share passwords or OTPs. A genuine PMS works through a demat account opened in your name under a signed agreement, not through your personal logins. Anyone asking for them is a red flag.

items.q: Where do I complain about a PMS or mutual fund?
items.a: First write to the firm's grievance officer. If it isn't resolved, use SEBI's SCORES complaint system, and the Online Dispute Resolution platform for market disputes.

items.q: What is an execution-only platform?
items.a: A SEBI framework from 2023 for platforms that only process Direct mutual fund transactions, without giving advice. They register with AMFI or as stock brokers.

items.q: Can I buy mutual funds on NIVO?
items.a: NIVO's investing flow is live in practice mode: you can build a basket, see checks before each order, and place practice orders. Live orders will start once NIVO is SEBI-registered and connected to BSE StAR MF. Each order already shows how to invest for real today, with no commission.

items.q: How will NIVO place my mutual fund orders?
items.a: Through BSE StAR MF in Direct plans only. Your money goes from your bank directly to the exchange's clearing corporation, never through NIVO, and units land in your own folio.

items.q: How do I invest in a PMS through NIVO?
items.a: Pick a strategy and tap Invest. NIVO checks it against your score and the ₹50 lakh minimum, then guides you to the manager's direct onboarding, with no distributor in between. You sign the agreement and open the account with the manager.

items.q: Why does NIVO only use Direct plans?
items.a: Because Direct plans don't pay commissions out of your returns. NIVO earns nothing from your orders, so it has no reason to push one fund over another.

items.q: What checks does NIVO run before I invest?
items.a: Whether it's a Direct plan, how well it fits your IPS or Investor Score, whether it's too aggressive for you, concentration in one holding, thematic limits, track record, and for PMS, the ₹50 lakh minimum and style fit. Blocking issues stop the order; warnings ask you to look again.

items.q: What do I need before my first order?
items.a: Completed KYC, a bank account in your name, UPI AutoPay or an e-mandate for SIPs, a nominee decision, and reading the risk disclosure. NIVO never asks for your passwords or full account numbers.

items.q: What is a mutual fund twin?
items.a: A mix of Direct mutual funds in the same style as a PMS strategy. It lets you follow a similar approach before you reach ₹50 lakh, with daily liquidity and lower costs. It copies the style, not the manager's exact stock picks.

items.q: What is the NIVO Investor Score?
items.a: A score out of 10 from 22 questions about your finances, horizon, risk appetite, behaviour in falls and knowledge. It decides which PMS strategies NIVO suggests. If what you say and what you'd actually do differ, NIVO goes with what you'd do.

items.q: How does NIVO pick my top 5 PMS?
items.a: It filters strategies with at least 3 years of record and a risk level your score allows, then ranks them on NIVO Score, risk fit, worst year against your comfort limit, calm and consistency, and your style preference, with one strategy per manager.

items.q: What is Commission X-ray?
items.a: A NIVO tool that finds every Regular plan in your portfolio and shows what its commission costs you per year and over 10 and 20 years, with the Direct twin to move to.

items.q: What is Panic guard?
items.a: A NIVO screen to read before selling in a fall. It shows what you told NIVO when markets were calm, how your holdings handled past falls, and your own rules, so you decide with a clear head.

items.q: What is Family readiness?
items.a: A NIVO checklist for nominees, a will and one list of all your accounts, scored out of 10. It helps make sure your family can find and claim your investments.

items.q: Is my data safe with NIVO?
items.a: On this version, your data stays in your own browser or your private Claude storage, and NIVO never asks for passwords or account numbers. When NIVO moves to its own servers, data will be encrypted and stored in India.

items.q: Does NIVO get paid by fund houses or PMS managers?
items.a: No. No commissions, no referral fees, no paid rankings. A better NIVO Score can't be bought.

items.q: How do I know if my wealth manager is giving good advice?
items.a: Check whether advice matches your IPS, whether costs are shown in rupees, how often products are switched, and whether recommendations lean to high-cost products. NIVO's pitch checker tests their claims against real data.

items.q: My RM wants me to switch funds every year. Is that normal?
items.a: Frequent switching without a written reason is a warning sign. Each switch can create tax and exit loads, and in Regular plans the switch can generate fresh commission. Ask for the reason in writing and check it against your IPS.

items.q: My RM is recommending a new fund offer (NFO). Should I buy?
items.a: An NFO has no track record and isn't cheaper because its NAV is ₹10. Unless it offers something genuinely new that fits your plan, an existing fund with a proven record is usually the better choice.

items.q: What questions should I ask my wealth manager?
items.a: How are you paid on what you recommend? What are all my costs in rupees? Why this product over a cheaper similar one? How does this fit my IPS? What would make you recommend selling it?

items.q: Is a structured product or market-linked debenture right for me?
items.a: They can be complex, with payoffs that depend on index levels, issuer credit risk and limited liquidity. Make sure you understand when you lose money and who you're lending to. If you can't explain it simply, don't buy it.

items.q: How do I fact-check a wealth manager's pitch deck?
items.a: Upload it to NIVO's Check a pitch. Each claim, like returns, ratings or comparisons, is tested against AMFI and PMS data, and missing disclosures are flagged.

items.q: What does a aggressive model portfolio look like?
items.a: NIVO's Aggressive model holds 80% equity and 20% debt: Nifty 50 index fund 25%, Flexi cap 20%, Large & mid cap 10%, Mid cap 15%, Small cap 10%, Short duration debt 8%, Target-maturity G-Sec/SDL 7%, Liquid 5%. Review when equity or debt drifts more than 5 points from target. It is a category framework, not personal advice.

items.q: What does a balanced model portfolio look like?
items.a: NIVO's Balanced model holds 60% equity and 40% debt: Nifty 50 index fund 20%, Flexi cap 15%, Large & mid cap 10%, Mid cap 10%, Small cap 5%, Short duration debt 15%, Corporate bond 10%, Target-maturity G-Sec/SDL 10%, Liquid 5%. Review when equity or debt drifts more than 5 points from target. It is a category framework, not personal advice.

items.q: What does a conservative model portfolio look like?
items.a: NIVO's Conservative model holds 25% equity and 75% debt: Nifty 50 index fund 10%, Flexi cap 10%, Large & mid cap 5%, Short duration debt 20%, Corporate bond 15%, Target-maturity G-Sec/SDL 15%, Banking & PSU debt 10%, Liquid 10%, Floating rate 5%. Review when equity or debt drifts more than 5 points from target. It is a category framework, not personal advice.
